tip_title: The Liability Limit on Your Home Policy Is Probably the Number You've Never Looked At
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: The Liability Limit on Your Home Policy Is Probably the Number You've Never Looked At**

Most homeowners policies come with $100,000 in personal liability coverage baked in by default. That sounds like a lot until you realize a single lawsuit — a guest who slips and falls, a dog bite, a neighbor's kid injured in your yard — can blow past that number fast. The liability section of your declarations page is worth a quick look, because a lot of people have never touched that number since they bought the policy. If your limit is sitting at $100,000 and your assets have grown since then, that gap matters.

Not sure if your liability limit still makes sense for where you are today? Your Peachy agent can pull up your declarations page and walk through it with you — takes about ten minutes.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/homeowners/learn/personal-liability-insurance-homeowners)
summary: Covers the personal liability limit embedded in standard homeowners policies — specifically that the default $100,000 limit may be inadequate for most households — framed as a declarations-page check rather than an umbrella purchase decision.
scoring_notes: Works for both audiences. East Cobb is 78% homeowners with higher assets; Perimeter is 55% homeowners but skews young professional with growing net worth. Lewisville Lake is 65% homeowners across a mix of income brackets. The declarations-page check angle is concrete and takes five minutes. Prior umbrella tips covered umbrella as a product and pool-specific liability — this is a different angle: the base homeowners liability limit itself as a neglected number. August timeliness is solid because summer hosting season (pools, gatherings) is still active, raising incident likelihood. Source is NerdWallet (trusted list). Not a repeat subject — prior tips focused on what umbrella covers and who needs it, not on the base policy liability limit as an overlooked default number.

tip_title: Late Summer Storms Are the Real Test. Does Your Policy Handle Hail the Way You Think?
topic: wind and hail damage home insurance
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Late Summer Storms Are the Real Test. Does Your Policy Handle Hail the Way You Think?**

Hail damage is one of the most common homeowners claims filed every year, and August storms in Georgia and North Texas are no joke. Here's the thing most people miss: even if your policy covers hail, the deductible structure might not work the way you expect. Some policies have a separate wind and hail deductible — a percentage of your dwelling coverage rather than a flat dollar amount — which means on a $350,000 home, a 1% deductible is $3,500 out of pocket before coverage kicks in. Pull up your declarations page and look for any line that says "wind," "hail," or "windstorm" deductible separately from your standard deductible.

Not sure which deductible applies to storm damage at your house? Your Peachy agent can walk through exactly how your policy reads.

📖 [Learn more from U.S. News](https://www.usnews.com/insurance/homeowners-insurance/does-homeowners-insurance-cover-hail-damage)
summary: Covers wind and hail coverage in homeowners policies with a focus on the separate wind/hail deductible structure — specifically the percentage-based mechanic and how to find it on the declarations page — as a late-summer storm-season check.
scoring_notes: August is peak severe weather season in both Georgia (East Cobb, Perimeter) and North Texas (Lewisville Lake). Hail is a top claim driver in DFW specifically. Prior tip on this subject (June 12) covered the percentage-deductible mechanic broadly — this tip sharpens the angle to the declarations-page lookup step and gives a concrete math example ($350k home, 1% = $3,500) to make the mechanic land. That's a meaningfully different instructional frame. High homeowner populations in all three newsletters. Timeliness score 9 because late August storms are active right now in both regions. Source is U.S. News — not on the primary trusted list but is a broadly credible consumer finance publisher; NerdWallet and III.org didn't have hail-specific candidates in the set. Used the best available source from candidates provided.
